newsitem.title: USA: U.S. investigates report of near air collision.
newsitem.headline: U.S. investigates report of near air collision.

text.p: The National Transportation Safety Board said on Friday it will investigate an incident off the New Jersey coast involving a jetliner and two national guard F-16 jet fighters that the charter jet's operator described as a near collision.

NTSB spokesman Paul Schlamm said the board will look into Wednesday's incident in which the Boeing 727 with about 80 passengers maneuvered violently in response to electronic cockpit warnings when it was approached by one F-16.

"We will be looking into that incident to see if we can make any recommendations on possible changes in the area," Schlamm told Reuters, adding that the NTSB probe would be independent of an Air Force investigation of the incident.

The Pentagon, meanwhile, denied the incident was a near miss, saying one of the two New Jersey Air National Guard jets had carefully flown to 1,000 feet (304.8 metres) behind and 1,000 feet (304.8 metres) below the Nations Air Boeing 727 en route from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to New York.

"I can't call it a near collision," Air Force Maj. Tom Schultz, a Defense Department spokesman, told Reuters on Friday. "The reaction of the civilian (airliner) pilots was in response to their collision warnings."

NBC television news, which first reported the incident on Thursday, quoted Mark McDonald, president of Smyrna, Georgia-based Nations Air, as saying the plane was forced to dive, climb and climb again to avoid a collision.
The airliner later landed safely at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.

"Our instrument indicated zero-zero, which means it was extremely close, because it was so close it did not read on the instrument," McDonald told NBC. "Either the pilots screwed up or they were playing games with our airplane, and they got caught."

But Col. Thomas Griffin, commander of the 177th Fighter Wing of the New Jersey Air National Guard, told Philadelphia ABC-TV affiliate WPVI: "There was no taunting. There was no frivolous play. There was no 'Top Gunning.' There was none of that. It was extremely professional."
Federal aviation officials said that no injuries were reported, but NBC said that two flight attendants and one passenger were thrown from their seats by the maneuvering.

The incident occurred shortly after 1:30 p.m. EST (1830 GMT) about 70 miles (115 km) east off Atlantic City, New Jersey, in an area that had been designated for training by the New Jersey Air National Guard.

Schultz said he understood that FAA civilian air traffic controllers in New York had given permission for the jetliner to fly through the area. That information was apparently then relayed to the F-16s by military traffic controllers.

Exact times were not immediately clear, but the lead plane of the F-16 flight reported that he was informed that there was a civilian airliner in the area at about the time that he spotted the plane 5 miles (8.047 km) away.

"The lead (fighter) aircraft continued to fly toward the civilian plane to confirm that it was the plane reported in the area," said Schultz. He said F-16 pilot did not realize that he had triggered automatic collision warnings on the passenger jet, but pulled away when he confirmed the identity of the big plane.
"It was a controlled, cautious approach toward the (passenger) aircraft," Schultz said.
The Pentagon said the inspector general of the First Air Force, with headquarters at Tyndall Air Force Base in Panama City, Florida, was conducting a full investigation of the incident.
The New Jersey Air National Guard is based in Atlantic City.
